title: Wall Street Books Weekly Gain Despite Bond Rout
content: US equities closed higher on Friday and secured weekly gains, shrugging off a punishing rise in Treasury yields as oil prices eased. The S&P 500 added 0.51% to 7,743.41, the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.48% to 27,068.72 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 478.64 points, or 0.93%, to 51,828.62, leaving all three benchmarks higher for the week even as the 10-year yield hovered near 5.2%.
summary: US stocks rose on Friday and finished the week higher, defying a jump in Treasury yields as crude prices retreated.
context:
• Markets are still adjusting to the Federal Reserve's September hike to a 3.75%-4% target range, its first increase since 2023.

• Elevated long-term yields have pressured richly valued megacap and growth names for much of the month.

• A retreat in oil, on hopes of a phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, helped calm inflation nerves into the weekend.
happened:
• The S&P 500 rose 0.51% to 7,743.41 and the Nasdaq gained 0.48% to 27,068.72.

• The Dow climbed 478.64 points, or 0.93%, to 51,828.62, with all three indices booking weekly gains.

• The advance came despite the 10-year Treasury yield lingering around 5.2%, near multi-year highs.
implications:
• With the Fed signalling further tightening, equities remain hostage to the path of yields.

• Continued relief in oil would ease the inflation impulse that has driven the bond sell-off.

• Any renewed spike in crude or long-end yields is the clearest threat to the rebound.
importance:
• The weekly gain shows dip-buying appetite has survived a bruising move in rates.

• Leadership in technology and growth is the most exposed if the long end reprices higher.

• Direction from here hinges on whether disinflation resumes or oil reignites price pressures.

title: 10-Year Yield Near 5.2% as Rate-Hike Bets Build
content: US Treasuries extended their sell-off, with the 10-year yield hovering around 5.2% on Friday, close to its highest level since 2007, as investors priced in the risk of further Federal Reserve tightening. Hawkish Fed commentary, a jump in University of Michigan inflation expectations and worries over rising government debt combined to push yields higher, with futures now implying a strong chance of another hike as soon as October.
summary: The 10-year Treasury yield sat near 5.2%, close to a multi-year high, as markets braced for more Fed tightening.
context:
• The Fed lifted rates to 3.75%-4% in September and updated projections point to the possibility of another increase this year.

• Oil above US$100 for much of the month has stoked fears that inflation will prove sticky.

• Strong US data, a widening deficit and heavy issuance have all weighed on the long end of the curve.
happened:
• The 10-year yield hovered around 5.2%, near its highest since 2007.

• The University of Michigan survey confirmed a sharp rise in inflation expectations in September.

• CME FedWatch pricing implied roughly a 75% chance of an October hike and around a 59% chance of a further move in December.
implications:
• Higher-for-longer yields raise borrowing costs across mortgages, corporate credit and government debt.

• A repricing of the front end would pressure rate-sensitive equities and lengthen the bond drawdown.

• Fiscal supply concerns could keep a structural premium in long-dated Treasuries.
importance:
• The 10-year yield is the global benchmark for the price of money, anchoring valuations across asset classes.

• A durable move above 5% marks a regime shift after years of ultra-low rates.

• Every inflation print and Fed speech is now a live catalyst for volatility.

title: Dollar Holds Near Two-Month High on Yield Surge
content: The US dollar held firm on Friday, with the dollar index staying above 101 and near its strongest level in nearly two months, on track for a second consecutive weekly gain. Rising Treasury yields widened the greenback's rate advantage, sending the euro and the yen to roughly 1.5-week lows, though the yen drew some support after Tokyo and Washington reaffirmed the stance underpinning July's joint interventions.
summary: The dollar held near a two-month high and headed for a second weekly gain as surging Treasury yields boosted its rate advantage.
context:
• Widening interest-rate differentials have underpinned the dollar as the Fed leans hawkish.

• The Bank of Japan raised rates to a 31-year-high 1.25% last week but offered cautious guidance, leaving the yen vulnerable.

• Joint US-Japan interventions in July set a reference point that authorities continue to defend.
happened:
• The dollar index held above 101, near its strongest in almost two months, on course for a second straight weekly rise.

• The euro and yen slipped to around 1.5-week lows against the dollar.

• Higher T-note yields strengthened the dollar's rate differentials into the weekend.
implications:
• A stronger dollar tightens global financial conditions and pressures emerging-market borrowers.

• Renewed yen weakness supports Japanese exporters but raises imported-energy costs.

• Sustained divergence between the Fed and other central banks could extend the dollar's advance.
importance:
• The dollar's direction reshapes corporate earnings, commodity prices and cross-border flows.

• Yen levels remain a key trigger for intervention risk and the global carry trade.

• FX moves are increasingly being driven by the US rates story rather than growth differentials.

title: Oil Slides on Hopes of Hormuz Reopening Deal
content: Crude prices fell on Friday as reports that US and Iranian negotiators are exploring a phased deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz eased acute supply fears. West Texas Intermediate settled around $92 a barrel and Brent near $104, pulling back sharply, though US crude still held gains of roughly 18% for the month after weeks of conflict-driven disruption to the vital waterway.
summary: Oil dropped on Friday as talks over a phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz eased supply concerns, though crude remained sharply higher on the month.
context:
• The 2026 Iran conflict has severely restricted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint for a large share of seaborne crude.

• The disruption has been described by the IEA as one of the largest supply shocks in the history of the oil market.

• Saudi Arabia has rerouted some exports to compensate for damaged infrastructure, adding to volatile price swings.
happened:
• WTI settled around $92 a barrel and Brent near $104, both down on the day.

• The falls followed reports that Washington and Tehran are weighing a phased arrangement to restore access through Hormuz.

• Despite Friday's drop, US crude was still up roughly 18% for the month.
implications:
• A confirmed reopening would relieve a major inflation driver and give central banks room to pause tightening.

• Any breakdown in talks or fresh attacks could send prices sharply higher again.

• Energy-heavy equity sectors and import-dependent economies remain acutely exposed to the outcome.
importance:
• Oil is the single biggest swing factor for global inflation and rate expectations right now.

• The Hormuz standoff links geopolitics directly to bond, FX and equity markets.

• Headline-driven crude moves are amplifying volatility across every asset class.

title: Gold Slips to $4,285 as Yields Trump Safe-Haven Bid
content: Gold eased to around $4,285 an ounce on Friday, extending a pullback that has seen the metal fall about 7% over the past month even as geopolitical tensions persist. Surging Treasury yields and a firmer dollar raised the opportunity cost of holding the non-yielding asset, offsetting safe-haven demand tied to the US-Iran conflict and leaving bullion well below the record above $5,000 struck in January.
summary: Gold slipped to about $4,285 an ounce as rising yields and a stronger dollar outweighed safe-haven demand.
context:
• Gold surged past $5,000 an ounce in January 2026 before a sustained retreat later in the year.

• Bullion typically struggles when real yields and the dollar rise, as the metal pays no income.

• The US-Iran conflict has kept a floor of safe-haven interest under precious metals.
happened:
• Gold traded around $4,285 an ounce, down roughly 7% over the past month but still up about 14% year on year.

• The decline persisted even as oil fell on Hormuz reopening hopes.

• Higher Treasury yields and dollar strength were the dominant drivers of the move.
implications:
• Further yield increases could keep gold under pressure despite geopolitical risk.

• A sharp escalation in the Middle East could quickly revive safe-haven flows.

• The metal's behaviour is a useful gauge of whether rates or risk dominate market sentiment.
importance:
• Gold is a key barometer of real rates, inflation expectations and geopolitical stress.

• Its slide despite conflict shows how powerfully the rates story is driving markets.

• Precious-metal moves matter for miners, central-bank reserves and multi-asset portfolios.

title: European Shares Snap Three-Week Losing Streak
content: European equities edged higher on Friday, with the pan-European STOXX 600 rising about 0.5% on the week to end a three-week losing run as falling oil prices eased pressure on the region's energy-intensive companies. Germany's DAX closed at 25,408.64, up 0.56% on the day, the FTSE 100 added 0.14% to 10,695.25 and France's CAC 40 dipped 0.04% to 8,077.80, with London lagging a firmer Frankfurt.
summary: The STOXX 600 rose about 0.5% for the week to break a three-week losing streak as easing oil lifted sentiment.
context:
• European markets had been rattled by a global bond rout and energy-driven inflation fears through September.

• The retreat in crude relieved pressure on energy-intensive industrials and rate-sensitive growth names.

• Long-term bond yields across the region remained elevated, capping the size of the rebound.
happened:
• The STOXX 600 gained roughly 0.5% for the week, snapping a three-week decline.

• The DAX closed at 25,408.64 (+0.56%), the FTSE 100 at 10,695.25 (+0.14%) and the CAC 40 at 8,077.80 (-0.04%).

• Frankfurt outperformed London, widening the gap between the two markets.
implications:
• Continued relief in energy and rates would support banks and cyclicals into quarter-end.

• A renewed spike in oil or yields remains the clearest risk to the recovery.

• The DAX's persistent outperformance keeps allocation questions in focus for Europe-weighted investors.
importance:
• European benchmarks have been among 2026's stronger performers, so their resilience matters for global allocators.

• The bounce signals that dip-buying appetite endured the month's volatility.

• Divergence between core and UK markets shapes relative-value positioning.

title: Nikkei Extends Winning Run as JGB Yields Hit 1996 High
content: Japanese stocks rallied for a fifth straight session on Friday, with the Nikkei 225 climbing 1.30%, or 850.21 points, to 66,364.20 and the broader TOPIX rising 1.31% to 4,128.59, buoyed by a weaker yen. The advance came even as Japan's 10-year government bond yield briefly touched 3.115%, its highest since 1996, while mainland China, South Korea and Taiwan were shut for the Mid-Autumn holiday and Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell about 1%.
summary: The Nikkei rose for a fifth day as a soft yen offset a jump in JGB yields to a near three-decade high, with much of Asia closed for holidays.
context:
• The Bank of Japan raised its policy rate to a 31-year-high 1.25% last week as it continues to normalise ultra-loose policy.

• A weaker yen flatters the earnings of Japan's large exporter base, supporting the Nikkei.

• Rising global yields have dragged Japanese government bond yields to levels unseen in decades.
happened:
• The Nikkei 225 gained 1.30% to 66,364.20 and the TOPIX rose 1.31% to 4,128.59, a fifth consecutive advance.

• Japan's 10-year JGB yield briefly hit 3.115%, its highest since 1996.

• Mainland China, South Korea and Taiwan were closed for the Mid-Autumn holiday, while the Hang Seng fell about 1% to 24,510.09.
implications:
• Further yen weakness would keep supporting exporters but sharpen imported-inflation pressures.

• Rising JGB yields could eventually lure Japanese capital home from overseas bond markets.

• Thin holiday liquidity across the region can exaggerate individual market moves.
importance:
• Japan's rate and currency path is a key driver of global funding conditions and the carry trade.

• A near-30-year high in JGB yields signals a profound shift in the world's former anchor of cheap money.

• Asian benchmarks set the tone for global risk appetite at the start of each trading day.

title: Bitcoin Retreats From Highs as Rate Fears Bite
content: Cryptocurrencies lost ground on Thursday, with Bitcoin falling to around $83,500 and Ether slipping to roughly $2,650, as mounting expectations of further Federal Reserve rate hikes sapped risk appetite. The pullback came just days after Bitcoin had touched near eight-month highs, with traders now assigning a strong probability to an October hike and a meaningful chance of another before year-end.
summary: Bitcoin fell to about $83,500 and Ether to roughly $2,650 as rising rate-hike expectations knocked digital assets back from recent highs.
context:
• Crypto rallied earlier in September, with Bitcoin approaching eight-month highs before the latest wobble.

• Digital assets have traded increasingly in step with rate-sensitive risk assets rather than as a hedge.

• Higher-for-longer rate expectations lift the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding tokens.
happened:
• Bitcoin fell around 2% to roughly $83,500, having opened Thursday near $84,370.

• Ether dropped about 2.5% to around $2,650.

• CME FedWatch pricing showed roughly a 75% chance of an October hike and about a 59% chance of a further move in December.
implications:
• Continued Fed hawkishness could cap the crypto recovery in the near term.

• Any dovish surprise or renewed disinflation would quickly revive risk appetite for digital assets.

• Tight correlation with equities leaves crypto exposed to the same rates-driven volatility.
importance:
• Bitcoin has become a high-beta gauge of global liquidity and risk sentiment.

• The retreat underscores how sensitive speculative assets are to the rate outlook.

• Crypto's swings increasingly ripple into equity and macro positioning.

title: Akamai Soars on $11.6bn Anthropic Cloud Deal
content: Shares in Akamai Technologies surged after the company unveiled an $11.6bn, seven-year cloud computing agreement with AI developer Anthropic, sending the stock up as much as 20% in after-hours trading before paring gains. The deal, which the company said could grow to around $20bn, includes a warrant giving Anthropic the right to acquire up to about 5% of Akamai through nonvoting convertible preferred stock at an exercise price of $111.33.
summary: Akamai shares jumped after it announced an $11.6bn, seven-year cloud deal with Anthropic that could expand to around $20bn.
context:
• Demand for AI compute has driven a wave of large, multi-year infrastructure contracts across the technology sector.

• Akamai has been repositioning its content-delivery network towards distributed cloud and AI workloads.

• Investors have rewarded companies able to secure long-dated, high-value AI revenue commitments.
happened:
• Akamai announced $11.6bn of contractual commitments from Anthropic over an initial seven-year term.

• Shares rose as much as 20% after hours, briefly touching $128.46 before easing back.

• The agreement includes a warrant convertible into up to roughly 5% of Akamai's stock at $111.33, vesting as Anthropic's spending grows.
implications:
• The contract gives Akamai a large, visible revenue stream and validates its AI-infrastructure pivot.

• The equity warrant aligns Anthropic with Akamai's performance but could dilute existing holders over time.

• Further hyperscaler and AI-lab deals could re-rate second-tier cloud providers.
importance:
• The deal is a fresh datapoint on the scale of AI infrastructure spending reshaping the tech sector.

• Long-dated commitments of this size can transform the earnings profile of mid-cap names.

• It highlights how AI demand is spreading beyond the megacap chipmakers to networking and cloud players.

title: Costco Tops Estimates on E-Commerce Surge
content: Costco Wholesale beat Wall Street expectations for its fiscal fourth quarter, reporting after the close on Thursday revenue of $95.7bn and diluted earnings of $6.75 a share, against consensus of about $94.85bn and $6.55. Net sales rose 11.2% to $93.9bn and comparable sales climbed 9.4%, powered by a 19.5% jump in digitally enabled sales, though results were flattered by a $0.15-a-share benefit from tariff refunds.
summary: Costco beat fiscal Q4 estimates with $95.7bn revenue and $6.75 EPS, helped by strong comparable and e-commerce sales.
context:
• Costco's membership model has proved resilient as consumers seek value amid sticky inflation.

• Retailers have been navigating shifting tariff policy, which has affected costs and refunds.

• The warehouse club has leaned into e-commerce to complement its store base.
happened:
• Revenue reached $95.7bn and diluted EPS was $6.75, up from $5.87 a year earlier, both beating consensus.

• Net sales rose 11.2% to $93.9bn, with comparable sales up 9.4% and digitally enabled sales up 19.5%.

• Results included a non-recurring $0.15-a-share benefit from tariff refunds; full-year net sales hit $297.2bn.
implications:
• Robust comps suggest consumer spending on essentials remains healthy despite high rates.

• Strong e-commerce growth points to a widening digital moat against discount rivals.

• The tariff-refund benefit means underlying earnings growth is slightly softer than the headline.
importance:
• Costco is a bellwether for US consumer resilience heading into the key holiday season.

• Its results feed directly into the debate over how much the Fed still needs to tighten.

• Consistent execution keeps the retailer a core holding across large-cap and consumer funds.
